name: Olga Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a fulfilment centre for an online clothes shop, the kind where you order three sizes and send two back. I don't walk the aisles any more. Little orange robots bring the shelves to my station, a light flashes on the bin, I pick the dress or the jeans, scan it and drop it in the order tote. On a good day I do about 300 picks an hour, and I'm on days, seven till half three.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: So robots are already part of your day. What's that like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Strange at first, now normal. My feet are thankful, because before the robots came in three years ago I was doing twenty thousand steps a shift. The bad part is you stand in one spot for hours and your shoulders seize up. Bea, who works the next station, and I stretch together at every break like two old women.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe now we can talk about the real stuff, like pay and breaks. I'd probably post something about how all those AI ads were mostly marketing. I'm in the union and we'd still want a better deal at the next pay round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things carry on, and I'm fine with that. I'm on decent pay, I've got about eight months saved towards a deposit, and there are loads of warehouses near the ring road if this one shuts. The robots I already work with aren't going anywhere either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving 350 a month towards the deposit for a flat. I'd maybe use the chatbot on my phone now and then, like I do to write an email to my landlord. And I'd push at the union meeting for a stretching break every two hours at the stations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit bored, maybe. Bored with eight months of savings is fine. I'll take the same station and the same orange robots for a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent. I pay 900 a month for a one-bedroom and it's gone up twice in two years. If nothing changes with AI, the landlord still puts it up, and the deposit gets further away every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bored. Would you look for something else anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in a couple of years. I've thought about the maintenance team, the ones who fix the robots when they get stuck. But I'd wait till someone I know has done it first and tells me it's worth it.

say: The **AI ads** were mostly marketing, so now people can talk about pay and breaks.
She'd still want the union to win a **better deal** at the next pay round.
think: With **eight months saved** and plenty of warehouses nearby, her work feels **secure**.
The **orange robots** she already works with would stay as they are.
do: Keep saving **350 a month** towards a flat deposit.
Use the phone chatbot now and then for **emails**, as she does now.
Ask the union for a **stretching break** every two hours at the stations.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **boredom** at the thought of the same station for years.
S0.quote: Bored with eight months of savings is fine. I'll take the same station and the same orange robots for a few more years.
fieldNote: She already works alongside **goods-to-person robots**, so robots feel ordinary to her.
Her real pressure is **rent rising** and the flat deposit moving away.
Interested in the **maintenance team**, but waits for proof from someone she knows.

steps.text: Keep saving 350 a month towards a flat deposit
Ask the union for a stretching break every two hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots spreading slowly is still robots spreading, and the union needs a plan before the next contract. Online I'd share stuff about retraining funds, because if the company saves money, some of it should go back to the people on the floor. I'd say it nicely, though, I'm not a shouter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the office goes first. The customer service team for returns, the people who write the product descriptions, they're in trouble now. For me it's the next step of robots, the arm that does the actual pick. They're testing one at the other site already, Bea's cousin saw it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager straight out if the maintenance team is hiring, and what the course costs. If two or three people from the floor got moved over and liked it, I'd apply. I'd keep saving, and I'd use the AI app a bit more to understand the robot error codes, since the engineers say it helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, because I've got savings and options. But I'd watch that test robot arm like it was a new manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the robot arm at the other site actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From what Bea's cousin said, it picks soft things out of a bin, like folded T-shirts, which used to be impossible. The robots that bring the shelves were slow too at the start. The robot arm at the other site is slower than me now, but not for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The returns team. Those women open every parcel, check for stains and decide if it goes back on sale. A camera with AI could do the checking part, and Fatima on returns has been there twelve years.

say: Robots spreading **slowly** is still robots spreading, so the union needs a **plan** now.
Some of what the company saves should fund **retraining** for people on the floor.
think: Returns customer service and **product writers** get hit first, before the pickers.
Her own risk is the **robot arm** being tested at another site.
do: Ask her manager whether the **maintenance team** is hiring and what the course costs.
Apply once **two or three** floor workers have moved over and liked it.
Use the AI app more to read **robot error codes**.
feel: **Uneasy** but not scared, because she has **savings and options**.
S1.quote: The robots that bring the shelves were slow too at the start. The robot arm at the other site is slower than me now, but not for long.
fieldNote: She tracks the **test robot arm** closely; the shelf robots taught her slow tech gets fast.
Her plan is a careful move to **robot maintenance**, but only after others prove it.
Worries about **returns staff** like Fatima (a long-serving colleague) before herself.

steps.text: Ask her manager about maintenance team openings and course costs
Use the AI app to learn robot error codes
Keep saving for the flat deposit at the same rate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an emergency and the government needs to act like it, with proper money for people losing work. I'd go to union meetings and sign every petition. And I'd tell my friends not to buy flats with big mortgages until we know what's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my station is gone by 2031 at the latest. The thinking stuff goes in 2028, so the planners and supervisors who run the site get replaced by software first, and then the arm that picks T-shirts gets good. I'd be thirty-one with no job and so would everybody near the ring road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the flat and keep the money as cash, because I wouldn't take on a mortgage. I'd get on the maintenance course in the first year even if I had to pay for it myself, because someone has to fix the robots for a while. And I'd look at work with people, like a care assistant, in case robots can't do that well yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, really anxious. But not hopeless, because I've got about eight months of money and three years before the robots. It's a race, and at least I can see the finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm not buying the flat, and she'd be upset because she's been asking about it for two years. Then I'd tell her I'm learning to fix robots, and she'd laugh, because I can't even fix her printer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to fix the robots for a while. How long is a while?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. If robots can do hands-on work as well as people in 2031, maybe they fix each other by 2033. Fixing robots is a bridge, not a career, but a bridge with good money while it lasts.

say: This is an **emergency**, and government needs **real money** for people losing work.
She'd tell friends not to buy flats with **big mortgages** until things settle.
think: Her station is **gone by 2031**, after the planners and supervisors go in 2028.
Every warehouse near the **ring road** would be cut at the same time.
do: Stop saving for the flat and keep the money as **cash**.
Take the **maintenance course** in the first year, paying for it herself if needed.
Look at **care work** as a fallback where people want people.
feel: **Really anxious**, but not hopeless, because she can see the **finish line**.
S2.quote: Fixing robots is a bridge, not a career, but a bridge with good money while it lasts.
fieldNote: She sees **2031** as the hard date for her station and plans backwards from it.
Gives up the **flat deposit dream** rather than take on a mortgage.
Her **eight months of savings** and youth keep her short of alarmed; she feels some control.

steps.text: Keep the flat deposit as cash instead of buying
Pay for the robot maintenance course in the first year
Apply for care assistant shifts as a backup
Sign union petitions for government support for laid-off workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if the government and companies actually plan. I'd be pushing the union for a deal where the company pays for retraining before anyone's laid off. I'd say it at work, calmly, and share the petitions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it gives me till about 2034 on the floor, so I'd be thirty-five. That's okay, actually. I could do the maintenance course, work on it a few years, and still have time to try something else after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see who from our site goes onto the maintenance team and how they find it, then apply. I'd keep saving for the flat, but for a smaller one, maybe 150 thousand instead of 200. And I'd use the AI app more for studying, since that's where the course stuff is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. Five years of warning feels like a long notice period. You don't love it, but you can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year rather than move straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's me. I'm not first in, ever. I want to hear from someone who's done the job before I spend my evenings on it. Bea's boyfriend is an engineer there, so I'd ask him first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the thinking parts of the site in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scheduling, the stock counts, the person who decides which orders go first, all that's AI by 2031. Honestly that might make my day easier at first. Fewer managers shouting about rates, more software just quietly setting them.

say: **Five years** is enough to do this properly, if government and companies **plan**.
The company should pay for **retraining** before anyone is laid off.
think: She'd have the floor until about **2034**, when she'd be thirty-five.
That leaves time for the **maintenance course** and another change after it.
do: Wait **a year** to see how colleagues find the maintenance team, then apply.
Aim for a **smaller flat**, around 150 thousand instead of 200.
Use the AI app more for **course study**.
feel: **Uneasy** more than scared, like a long notice period she can plan around.
S3.quote: Five years of warning feels like a long notice period. You don't love it, but you can plan.
fieldNote: Her steady nature shows: **never first in**, she waits for proof from people she knows.
Shrinks the **flat target** rather than abandoning it.
Expects AI scheduling might make her day **easier** at first.

steps.text: Apply to the maintenance team after a year of watching colleagues
Lower the flat target to about 150 thousand and keep saving
Study the maintenance course material with the AI app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so let's use them to make it fair. I'd want a law that companies share robot savings with workers, maybe through a shorter week. I'd say that at work and in the union chat, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is a long time for me. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes and forty when robots do the picking. That's a whole second career's worth of time if I start in my early thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the smaller flat in the next year or two while I've got a steady job, because a mortgage is easier to get now than later. I'd move to the maintenance team in a couple of years, and later maybe train as a nurse, because people will still want a person holding their hand. And I'd keep saving a bit every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a quiet way. It's there, like the rent going up, but it isn't keeping me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy the flat now if things change later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by 2039 I'd want a home that's mine, not a landlord's. If the money gets tight, at least nobody can put the rent up. My dad always says own your roof, and for once I agree with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt's a nurse and she says the job is half lifting and half talking. Robots might do the lifting, but I don't think anyone wants a robot telling them their test results. I don't know that for sure, it's a guess.

say: Ten years should be used to make the change **fair** for workers.
Companies should share robot savings, perhaps through a **shorter week**.
think: She'd be **forty** when robots pick, leaving time for a **second career**.
Ten years feels **long** enough to start again in her early thirties.
do: Buy the **smaller flat** in the next year or two while her job is steady.
Move to the **maintenance team** within a couple of years.
Consider **nurse training** later, for work where people want a person.
feel: **Uneasy** in a quiet way, like rising rent, but not keeping her awake.
S4.quote: Robots might do the lifting, but I don't think anyone wants a robot telling them their test results.
fieldNote: Ten years flips her plan: she'd **buy the flat** now rather than hold cash.
Thinks about a **people job** like nursing, honestly calling it a guess.
Her views stay **progressive** but her tone is calm and practical.

steps.text: Buy a smaller flat within two years while the job is steady
Move to the robot maintenance team in a couple of years
Look into nurse training through her aunt's hospital

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to watch other people try things first, and that's how I make decisions. What would help is free courses that start right away, and a promise from government that rent and mortgages won't swallow people while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who can't move. I've got savings and no kids. Bea has a son and no car, and she can only work at our site because it's on her bus route. Plans like mine don't work for her.

headlineQuote: I'm not first in, ever. I want to hear from someone who's done the job before I spend my evenings on it.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old picker** at an online clothes warehouse, where **shelf robots** already serve her station.
She rents, has about **eight months saved** towards a flat, and is a steady union member.
She waits for **proof** from others before changing, and plans a move to **robot maintenance**.
The **2-year AGI** picture makes her anxious; with ten years she'd buy a small flat and consider nursing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to see others try new paths first.
whatWouldHelp: **Free courses** that start at once, and protection from **rent** pressure while retraining.
